stories.title: Your guide to GitHub Universe 2026 is here: The schedule just launched!
stories.snippet: The GitHub Universe session catalog is live. Explore interactive workshops, community talks, demos, and panels. Plus, register before August 19 to save $300. The post Your guide to GitHub Universe 2026 is here: The schedule just launched! appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: GitHub Universe 2026 will take place October 28-29 at Fort Mason Center in San Francisco, featuring two days of sessions on AI-powered development with speakers from companies including AMD, Figma, NVIDIA, Coinbase, Anthropic, and OpenAI. Early Bird registration is available through August 19 and saves $300, with group discounts available on top of that. The schedule includes hands-on sessions covering Copilot configuration, stacked pull requests, fine-grained authorization for hosted MCP servers, and GitHub's agentic pipeline that manages 50+ services, alongside panels on the future of AI-assisted development. Other highlights include community-building talks, a session on building Home Assistant in the open with 20,000 contributors, and a demonstration of Copilot CLI hooks controlling a desk lamp. Three breakout sessions are competing for a main-stage spot, with public voting open until August 21.

stories.title: What 50 open source projects taught us about security in the AI era
stories.snippet: See how the open source projects in Session 4 of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund combined AI-assisted workflows, maintainer expertise, GitHub security tools, expert guidance, and funding to improve project security. The post What 50 open source projects taught us about security in the AI era appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: The GitHub Secure Open Source Fund Session 4 invested more than $500,000 across 50 open source projects, pairing maintainers with GitHub Security Lab experts, security tools, AI-assisted workflows, and a peer community. Each session runs as a three-week sprint with twelve months of follow-up, and every project receives $10,000 USD via GitHub Sponsors, broken into $6,000 during the sprint and $2,000 at six- and twelve-month check-ins. Training covers foundations of open source security, threat modeling and secure coding, and AI security and vulnerability management. The 50 participating projects were grouped into five categories spanning AI and machine learning infrastructure, build systems, core programming languages, developer tools, and web and networking services. OpenClaw participated as GitHub's fastest-growing open source project, using the program to develop an incident response plan, expand security tooling usage, and audit its GitHub Actions workflows. The program found that AI security is increasingly integrated into the broader practice of building secure software rather than evolving in isolation. Applications for Session 5 are open through August 24.

stories.title: GitHub availability report: July 2026
stories.snippet: In July, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services. The post GitHub availability report: July 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: GitHub's July 2026 availability report acknowledged an unacceptable GitHub Actions incident on August 6 and outlined accelerated migration of the service to Azure. In July, monolith read traffic in Azure Central US peaked at 52.75% on July 28, Git traffic in Azure reached 47% (up from 43% in June), and 29% of repositories gained a second replica in Central US. Authentication tables began moving off GitHub's oldest shared database, with the dedicated user service now offloading over one million queries per second at peak and 80% of a major authorization lookup shifted to an isolated path. Two significant incidents occurred: a 7-hour, 4-minute outage on July 8 affecting multiple services across data-resident Enterprise Cloud environments after a configuration safeguard failure, and a 9-hour, 18-minute GitHub Actions disruption on July 9. GitHub set a target of 70% read traffic and 30% write traffic in Central US this quarter, with a goal of moving all dotcom production traffic out of its data centers by end of 2026.

stories.title: Track generative AI costs with Amazon Bedrock inference profiles
stories.snippet: Learn how to track generative AI costs by department using Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles and AWS cost allocation tags. Create tagged profiles for each team and view per-department cost breakdowns in AWS Cost Explorer.
stories.summary: When multiple teams share a single foundation model in Amazon Bedrock, costs appear as one line item, making per-department chargeback and budgeting impossible. Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles solve this by acting as tagged wrappers around a foundation model that route usage to specific teams. To implement it, you create an inference profile for each department, tag it with a cost allocation tag like Team=HR, activate the tag in the AWS Billing console, and update your application to pass the profile ARN as the modelId parameter. The single IAM role remains unchanged, but Cost Explorer groups costs by team using the profile tags. The same per-token rate applies whether invoking the model directly or through a profile, and tagged costs take 24–48 hours to appear. For larger deployments, the AWS::Bedrock::ApplicationInferenceProfile CloudFormation resource lets you provision profiles at scale.

stories.title: Recovery strategies to meet data residency requirements
stories.snippet: Learn three strategies for achieving disaster recovery while meeting data residency requirements. Ranging from encryption-based controls on multi-Region replication to fully in-country architectures, these patterns help you balance recovery objectives with regulatory constraints.
stories.summary: Data residency requirements affect how government agencies, regulated industries, and businesses plan for the recovery of critical workloads on AWS. AWS offers multiple Regions within countries including the United States, Canada, Australia, India, Japan, Germany, China, and across the EU to support national-level residency needs. For residency requirements scoped to a country with a single AWS Region, three alternative strategies are available. Strategy 1, the cryptographic boundary, replicates data to a geopolitically aligned country using AWS KMS encryption with key policies that explicitly deny decryption in the recovery Region. Strategy 2, the data boundary, uses AWS Outposts at an on-premises site within the source country, with control planes hosted in a different parent Region. Strategy 3, the strict local autonomy boundary, keeps customer data and control plane systems within national borders through on-premises infrastructure or fully in-country AWS architectures. Continuous end-to-end testing is critical to building confidence that the chosen recovery strategy will work when required.

stories.title: Enhancing Virtual Agents through SLMs and Edge-Computing: An Exploratory Evaluation of Think and Memory Processes
stories.snippet: Embodied intelligent virtual agents are expected to operate as persistent, adaptive, and context-aware entities within complex virtual and Metaverse worlds. However, implementing cognitively capable agents in such environments is conceptually and technologically challenging. Among a range of blueprints and development approaches, the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) has been developed as an implementation-oriented framework for architecting components of perception, memory, reasoning, planning, and embodied action. Considering the recent advances in edge computing and generative AI
stories.summary: This paper explores how virtual agents can be enhanced through the integration of Small Language Models (SLMs) with edge-computing architectures. Rather than relying on large, cloud-based models, the authors examine how compact models deployed locally can support the reasoning and memory demands of conversational agents. The study provides an exploratory evaluation of "think" and "memory" processes, assessing how well SLMs handle deliberation and contextual recall when running on edge devices. By moving computation closer to the user, the approach aims to reduce latency, improve privacy, and lower operational costs while maintaining meaningful agent performance. The findings suggest that thoughtful design of reasoning and memory workflows can make SLMs a viable foundation for responsive virtual agents.

stories.title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
stories.snippet: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of improving models, systems, and other technical artifacts through long-horizon experimentation. To understand the current state of this capability, however, evaluation must go beyond final scores, which neither reveal where progress is gained or lost nor indicate whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. We therefore present a systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks based on a new framework that uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior through Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback
stories.summary: This paper addresses limitations in how AI agents are evaluated for long-horizon research and development tasks, arguing that final outcome scores alone provide an incomplete picture of agent capability. The authors propose a systematic evaluation framework that examines intermediate behaviors, decision-making trajectories, and the quality of processes leading to results, rather than relying solely on end-task metrics. The work likely benchmarks multiple AI agents performing extended research workflows such as hypothesis generation, experimentation, and code development, analyzing where agents succeed, fail, or exhibit inefficiencies. By dissecting performance across the research pipeline, the study aims to identify specific bottlenecks and failure modes that aggregate scores obscure. The contribution helps researchers design more diagnostic evaluations, enabling fairer comparisons between agents and clearer guidance for improving autonomous AI research systems.

stories.title: Deliberate Practice: Learning Robot Skills under a Budget
stories.snippet: We consider the problem of autonomously learning robot skills under a limited practice budget for sequential tasks. We propose an active skill learning algorithm, \emph{Deliberate Practice (DP)}, that computes a provably \emph{budget-optimal} allocation---practicing skills that maximize expected cumulative reward while being learnable within the budget. DP estimates both the time needed to master skills and the cumulative reward of the task plans that the skills unlock. Computing a budget-optimal allocation is challenging as it requires reasoning about combinatorially many skill plans over a l
stories.summary: Shivam Vats, Sudarshan Harithas, Mete Tuluhan Akbulut, Arvind Raghunathan, and George Konidaris propose Deliberate Practice (DP), an active skill learning algorithm that enables robots to autonomously learn skills under a limited practice budget for sequential tasks. DP computes a provably budget-optimal allocation by estimating both the time needed to master each skill and the cumulative reward of the task plans those skills unlock, practicing only those skills that maximize expected cumulative reward while remaining learnable within the budget. The key technical contribution is a bilinear program formulation that exactly computes this optimal allocation using off-the-shelf solvers, addressing the challenge of reasoning over combinatorially many skill plans over a large practice budget. Through simulated and real-world experiments on long-horizon manipulation tasks, the authors demonstrate that DP allows robots to optimally use limited practice time to acquire useful policies and improve long-horizon planning.

stories.title: Who Speaks Matters: Authority-Aware Multi-View RAG over Italian Parliamentary Proceedings
stories.snippet: Parliamentary proceedings are a primary record of democratic deliberation, yet their volume and fragmentation make multi-perspective access difficult for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to parliamentary transcripts introduces three specific risks: dominance of the most frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers according to topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text. We present ParliamentRAG, a RAG system for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that addresses these risks jointly. Its core contribution is a
stories.summary: ParliamentRAG is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system designed for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that addresses three challenges specific to parliamentary transcripts: the dominance of frequent speakers, the inability to weigh speakers by topical expertise, and citation misattribution. At its core, the system uses a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority relative to the current query by combining interpretable features such as profession, education, and previous interventions. Given a user query, the system retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a summary synthesizing their perspectives alongside supporting quotations. The authors evaluated ParliamentRAG against Google NotebookLM on 15 policy topics using a two-level protocol that combined automated metrics with blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts. ParliamentRAG achieved higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remained stronger on prose-oriented dimensions. The paper was accepted at the ISWC 2026 In-Use Track.

stories.title: Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model
stories.snippet: Existing predictive models in learning analytics often treat student academic history as a simple sequence, overlooking the concurrent nature of courses taken within a semester. This simplification can lead to inaccurate performance predictions, particularly for students with heavy or challenging course loads. This paper introduces a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation (TRACE) that addresses this limitation by jointly predicting both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for an upcoming semester. Our approach encodes courses on a per-semester basis
stories.summary: Paul Savala introduces TRACE (TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation), a model that addresses limitations in existing learning analytics systems, which treat student academic history as a simple sequence and overlook the concurrent nature of courses taken within a semester. The transformer-based approach jointly predicts both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for an upcoming semester, encoding courses on a per-semester basis to capture concurrency effects. It uses a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction. Trained on ten years of institutional data, the joint prediction model reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture that predicts grades alone, and outperforms both traditional LSTM-based sequential models and graph neural network-based approaches. The model offers natural ways to incorporate student attribute data and can be adapted to new institutions through retraining and recalibration, making it suitable for early detection systems at higher education institutions.

stories.title: Spaghettifying DRAM
stories.summary: The skitter-creek-bath-salts project targets AMD Family 16h CPUs, the last generation whose datasheets document the DRAM controller's translation registers and show they cannot be locked. It operates at the deepest layer of the *p pipeline — the memory controller (MCT/DCT) — where physical addresses are finally rewritten into raw DRAM coordinates before reaching the DIMM. By flipping a single bit in a DRAM controller register, such as the bank-swizzle-mode, the project rewires the physical-to-DRAM translation, scrambling platform memory and exposing protected DRAM regions invisible to the kernel. Because PSP, SMM, microcode, and C6 DRAM protection sit above the memory controller and guard physical addresses rather than DRAM coordinates, rearranging the coordinates bypasses all of them. The exploit disables APs, disables interrupts, flushes the target, rewires the controller, reads from the protected region, then restores the original mappings, keeping the platform operational while protected memory is exposed.

stories.title: Single log line is 49KB+ (ext4) / 110KB+ (btrfs) of systemd-journald disk writes
stories.summary: A bug report filed against systemd on January 3, 2026, details excessive disk I/O caused by systemd-journald on Debian 13 with systemd version 257.9. The reporter found that writing just two log lines per second generated approximately 50 IOPS on a virtual machine using XFS, with the title indicating a single log line results in 49KB+ of disk writes on ext4 and 110KB+ on btrfs. The expected behavior was log writes within an order of magnitude of syslog, but the actual journald output was far more I/O-intensive due to its inefficient storage format. The issue duplicates a previously closed ticket (#15292), which the reporter argues was dismissed without proper justification. Examples of repetitive haproxy log entries were provided to demonstrate the workload. The reporter also noted that journald files are significantly larger than the actual data written and that the format has proven unreliable after unclean reboots.

stories.title: Show HN: MCP Memory – Fast Agent Memory Using Google's OKF and SQLite FTS5
stories.summary: MCP-Memory is a Model Context Protocol server that gives AI agents persistent, long-term memory across sessions. It stores records using Google's Open Knowledge Format (OKF v0.2) Markdown standard and indexes them with a local SQLite instance using FTS5 full-text search, enabling sub-20ms key lookups and instant keyword searches. The system uses a dual-layer architecture, syncing every memory to disk as human-browseable .md files while maintaining a high-performance SQLite index, and supports namespace isolation for contextual separation. It exposes tools including memory_store, memory_retrieve, memory_search, memory_get_last, and memory_update_last, with the last two functioning as agent directives for session checkpoints. An interactive setup wizard auto-configures popular MCP clients like Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, and Codex, and by default creates project-isolated stores inside each project's root directory, with environment variables available for customizing paths.
